work.title: QUESTION LAB
work.subtitle: 问题实验室
work.scope: Fictional adult learning exercises. Illustrations are not records of real participants or research evidence. No accredited qualification or actual learner outcomes are supplied.

pages.title: Start with a noticed difference.
pages.lead: This inquiry course practises moving from a visible detail to a question that can be investigated. Use the fictional library scene as a prompt, not as research evidence.
pages.body: An adult learner notices two differently coloured notebooks. The colour is visible; who uses them and why are unknown. The first task is to keep those statements separate.
pages.detail: Working record: Record two visible details and one thing the picture cannot tell you. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Record two visible details and one thing the picture cannot tell you.

pages.title: Build a question tree.
pages.lead: Put one broad curiosity at the root and divide it into smaller questions. Each branch should ask for a different kind of information rather than repeat the same judgement.
pages.body: Root: how might a study corner support discussion? Branches might concern the purpose of the session, the material people use and how they choose a place to sit. None is established by a picture.
pages.subheading: Root question / three branches / one selected leaf
pages.detail: Working record: Write a root question, three branches and the narrowest question worth pursuing first. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write a root question, three branches and the narrowest question worth pursuing first.

pages.title: Make an assumption card.
pages.lead: An assumption is a provisional explanation, not a finding. Give it a short name and record what you expect to observe if it were useful.
pages.body: Assumption A: a shared sketch might help a discussion stay focused. A possible observation is whether speakers refer to the same sketch. Other explanations, such as a facilitator prompt, must remain visible.
pages.detail: Working record: Complete one card without using the words proven or always. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Complete one card without using the words proven or always.

pages.title: Request the evidence you need.
pages.lead: A useful evidence request names the question, the kind of material required and the limit of what that material could support. Do not collect personal data for this exercise.
pages.body: For the shared-sketch question, an invented transcript with references to objects would be more relevant than a photograph of an attractive room. A transcript still would not establish a causal effect.
pages.detail: Working record: Write an evidence request that another learner could understand without seeing your notes. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write an evidence request that another learner could understand without seeing your notes.

pages.title: Try a paper experiment.
pages.lead: Use two short invented dialogue extracts to practise applying the same rule. This is a desk exercise in consistent reading, not an experiment involving real participants.
pages.body: Extract A: I mean the left-hand shape. Extract B: I prefer this version. Code whether each sentence explicitly refers to a shared object. Keep the original wording beside your code.
pages.detail: Working record: Apply one coding rule to both extracts and flag any ambiguous phrase. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Apply one coding rule to both extracts and flag any ambiguous phrase.

pages.title: Compare without inventing a winner.
pages.lead: A comparison should show the criterion before the judgement. If the material is too thin, an unresolved result is more useful than a confident ranking.
pages.body: Sentence A names a shape; sentence B names a preference. That difference supports a description of the sentences, not a conclusion about which group learned more.
pages.subheading: Criterion / example A / example B / bounded conclusion
pages.detail: Working record: Write a comparison that stays within what the two extracts actually contain. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write a comparison that stays within what the two extracts actually contain.

pages.title: Invite a challenge.
pages.lead: Peer feedback should identify a claim, ask which material supports it and offer one alternative reading. The aim is to improve the inquiry rather than evaluate a person.
pages.body: A peer might ask whether left-hand refers to a shared diagram or only the speaker’s page. That question exposes a missing context which the coding rule should acknowledge.
pages.subheading: Claim under review / challenge / missing context
pages.detail: Working record: Write one generous challenge and the exact passage it addresses. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Write one generous challenge and the exact passage it addresses.

pages.title: Show your revision.
pages.lead: Keep the earlier wording visible beside the revision so a reader can see which assumption changed. Revision is a traceable decision rather than a replacement of the record.
pages.body: Earlier: the shared sketch improved discussion. Revised: one invented sentence explicitly names a shape, while the setting and effect on discussion remain unknown.
pages.detail: Working record: Revise one claim and name the evidence boundary that prompted the change. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Revise one claim and name the evidence boundary that prompted the change.

pages.title: Transfer the method.
pages.lead: Apply the inquiry sequence to a different fictional scene. Transfer means retaining the reasoning steps while changing the subject, not copying the previous conclusion.
pages.body: In a courtyard illustration, a learner notices an empty chair. Start with a question about what context is missing; do not infer low attendance, exclusion or preference from the empty seat.
pages.subheading: New detail / new question / source request
pages.detail: Working record: Draft a fresh question tree for an object outside the library example. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Draft a fresh question tree for an object outside the library example.

pages.title: Keep an inquiry record.
pages.lead: Finish with a compact account of the route you took: noticed detail, selected question, assumption, source request and revised claim. A useful record includes an unresolved question.
pages.body: This course provides no grade or accredited qualification. Its outcome is a more inspectable piece of reasoning and a clear account of which evidence you still do not have.
pages.subheading: Detail / question / assumption / revision / next source
pages.detail: Working record: Choose the strongest revision in your record and explain why it is more careful. Keep your first attempt and your revised version so the change remains visible.
pages.question: Choose the strongest revision in your record and explain why it is more careful.
